families.answer:
The erosion filter wins, but at 2 stripe octaves with an altitude fade, not at the prototyper's 5. That form costs 25.6 ns with a generic Source (forward differences) or 20.3 ns with an analytic internal base, against 50.3 and 44.9 ns at 5 octaves. These are AVX2 numbers from my own harness (t_gully_avx2), which calibrates to real fnlab within about 10 percent: perlin .92 vs .91, FBm3 3.47 vs 3.34, FBm5 simplex 6.67 vs 6.04, ridged6 W1 6.52 vs 6.58. It is intrinsics, not a FastSIMD port.

Same-base AVX2 costs, 5 detail octaves unless stated:
- Ridged detail: 9.3 ns
- Uber detail: 11.4 ns
- Slope-aligned detail: 12.2 ns
- Swiss detail: 14.9 ns
- Erosion: 12.4 ns analytic / 17.7 ns FD at 1 octave, 20.5 / 25.9 at 2, 28.6 / 34.1 at 3, 44.9 / 50.3 at 5. One stripe octave costs about 8.1 ns.

Where I disagree with the prototyper:
1. The same-base sheets were not a fair comparison. The same str is not the same amplitude: rms(delta) was ridged .066, uber .021, swiss .030, slope aligned .061, erosion 2 oct .119, and erosion's delta also has mean +.10. I re-rendered with amplitudes matched (gullies_fair_rms_matched_s7/s99). Ridged, uber and slope aligned become spikes, Swiss becomes lumps, and erosion still shows coherent gullies. So the win holds, and it is not an amplitude effect.
2. The filter's flats and valleys were not smooth as reported. The relief shows valley floors as rough as the flanks. A smoothstep on source height applied to the mask, plus a fade target, fixes this at no cost (25.63 vs 25.89 ns). On seed 7 at 3 octaves, max flow accumulation went from 1848 to 13775 and pits from 4.74 to 3.39. This changed the look more than anything else I tried. Only the target needs to be inside the node, and in-node the fade avoids extra Source evaluations.
3. 5 octaves are wasted. With the fade, 1 octave already shows bold gully ribs, 2 is the knee with branching, and 3 is only slightly crisper.
4. "Base must be smooth" holds only for a narrow stencil. A forward-difference stencil of .2, about the gully wavelength, low-passes a rough source: fbm5 c0 3.48 to 7.14, ridged4 c0 1.25 to 6.54. So the node can take any Source, which matters because FastNoise has no analytic gradients.
5. 4D is not a dead end. A hypercubic 4D lattice reads as a + weave, but a 4D Gen that recovers the torus angles and runs the wrapped 2D lattice tiles exactly (c0 7.28, no seam in the 2x2 view). This is proven in scalar only, and the 4D cost of about 56 ns is an estimate.

Hessian (perlin2h): tested three uses and none pays. The plan curvature mask gives wormy hairlines (c0 2.51). The direction-stability mask is amplitude invariant but softer with fewer gullies. Curved phase only helps very big cells. A generic Source would need 6 evaluations for any of them.

Lattice imprint: a square lattice has |c4| .23 to .29 at the first octave, and a triangular one has |c6| .13 to .15. Triangular reduces the imprint and makes it 6 fold; it does not remove it. The first critic's axis4 metric could not see 6 fold.

Cheaper tiers, if gullies are not strictly needed:
- Swiss on its own base (11.5 ns, 1.77x ridged, 45 percent of erosion) gives long parallel flutes on steep walls, so "no mode produces gullies" is too strong, but they do not branch.
- A real node graph of ridged plus altitude fade (12.9 ns) gives good rugged terrain with smooth valleys and no new node, but no gullies.
- Slope-aligned loses outright: 12.2 ns against 12.4 ns for one erosion octave, and it shows needle grass.

Remaining erosion weaknesses: at wide views the gullies are short dashes of one size, 3D is a heightfield only, and gully scale must be set against hill scale.

The gallery was already overwritten by an earlier critic pass, so I treated its critic.json as unverified too and kept those as critic.prev1.json. I agree with it on Uber being FractalRidged W=1. I disagree on 3 stripe octaves, on axis4 proving the imprint gone, and on folding slope-aligned into fractal-derivative (Swiss needs Perlin, c0 1.81 on Simplex, and slope-aligned needs Simplex).
families.proto_answer:
Which terrain gully method wins per ns: the erosion-filter is the only one of the three that actually makes gullies, and it wins the family outright on look; the other two do not compete on gullies at all, so per-ns comparison is really "pay 24x Perlin for gullies, or pay about 1x ridged for smooth valleys". Measured on one shared base (perlin octaves at seed+i, bf 0.7, window 3, same seed;

- Plain ridged FBm (fractal-derivative mode 0 sharp -1, no feedback): 520 ns scalar, 10.6x perlin2. Rough everywhere, no organisation.
- fractal-derivative (Uber ridge + slope + altitude erosion): 538 ns, 10.9x perlin, only 3 percent over plain ridged, c0ratio 7.7, 2D+3D work. Relief: smooth sediment bowls and flats with all detail on crests and rims; Swiss (481 ns, 9.8x, c0 4.0 from steep crests) gives knife crests and smooth valleys; Jordan gives billowy domes. No mode produces gullies or drainage lines. It is a keeper for what it does (smooth valleys/detailed crests, a look ridged+graphs cannot make, nearly free), but it is not a gully method.
- fractal-slope-aligned (elliptical-kernel simplex, frame from octave 0): 469 ns, 9.2x perlin, actually slightly cheaper than the plain simplex FBm in the same harness (505 ns), c0ratio 8.0, 2D+3D work. Relief: fluted slopes with thin straight downhill fibres fanning from peaks; reads as downhill grain, not as nested or branching gullies. Strata mode gives contour-wrapping flow-marble bands, the most novel texture in the family. Two honest failures inside it: the catalogue's coordinate-stretch form is broken (c0 1.2, maxSlope 667, scribbles), and letting anisotropic octaves steer later frames compounds into near-jumps (c0 6.9 at 2 octaves, 2.0 at 3), so the frame may only use the first octave (fo=1), which means detail does not nest as the spec promised. Promising, best folded into fractal-derivative as a Frame mode.
- erosion-filter (3-octave base + 5 phacelle stripe octaves, sf 0.6, branch 0.3, str 0.15, s0 0.15): 1200 ns, 24.3x perlin (4 octaves: 1042 ns, 20.7x), c0ratio 6.3, far coords fine, 3D heightfield form works (plane lattice). Relief: hill flanks carved by parallel V gullies with finer tributaries feeding coarser ones, dendritic dark lines in hillshade converging into smooth valleys. Clearly the most convincing terrain, and nothing else in the family or on the existing sheet comes close. Conditions: the base must be smooth (a 5-octave fractal base scrambles the stripes into spikes, measured), one stripe per cell gives starbursts and branch 1 gives herringbone, so defaults must ship as found. Phacelle 3x3 polynomial cells look identical to the 4x4 exp window in relief; finite-difference gradients looked identical to analytic ones at eps 0.01, so the Bevy warning did not bite on a smooth base.

Verdict: ship erosion-filter as the gully node (with phacelle-noise inside it as the Stripes output), ship fractal-derivative as the cheap smooth-valley/crest-detail fractal, and keep fractal-slope-aligned as a Frame mode candidate for fractal-derivative rather than a gully competitor. Estimated AVX2 (not measured, scaled from scalar ratios): erosion ~25-40 ns 2D, fractal-derivative ~8-10 ns 2D / ~16-20 ns 3D, slope-aligned ~6-8 ns 2D / ~14 ns 3D.
challenged: Erosion AVX2 25-40 ns at 5 stripe octaves, 3-5 ns per stripe octave (estimates): measured 44.9 ns analytic and 50.3 ns forward difference at 5 octaves, about 8.1 ns per stripe octave.
Fractal-derivative only 3 percent over plain ridged: a scalar artefact. AVX2 harness: uber 9.19 ns, swiss 11.52 ns, ridged 6.52 ns, so 1.41x and 1.77x.
Fractal-derivative is 'a look ridged plus graphs cannot make': false for Uber. Real FractalRidged Weighted=1 gives the same crests and bowls at 6.58 ns.
'No mode produces gullies': too strong. Swiss on its own base gives long parallel downhill flutes on steep walls at warp .15-.3, though they do not branch.
Slope-aligned slightly cheaper than plain simplex FBm: scalar early-out artefact. AVX2 without early out: 7.99 ns vs 6.67 ns, 1.20x.
Erosion hillshade 'converging into smooth valleys, flats stay smooth from the slope mask': the relief shows valley floors as rough as the flanks. Only an added altitude mask makes them smooth.
'The base must be smooth': true only with a narrow stencil. A .2 forward-difference stencil takes fbm5 c0 3.48 to 7.14 and ridged4 c0 1.25 to 6.54.
5 stripe octaves as the recommended default: 2 octaves nearly match it at half the cost once the altitude fade is on.
Same-base comparison at equal str: amplitudes differ up to 5.7x (rms delta uber .021 vs erosion 2 oct .119).
3x3 polynomial 'identical' to the 4x4 window taken as a clean result: both square lattices carry an unreported + weave, |c4| .23-.29 at the first octave.
Fractal-derivative vol 'solid 3D lobes': at iso 0 it is almost solid with a few holes, because the mean is about +.3 to +.4.
Slope-aligned 3D 'streaky surfaces': the vol shows pockmarked surfaces with dots.
Aniso-simplex-steered c0ratio 8.0: measured 6.38 with max slope 56 at seed 42.
Erosion '3D heightfield form works' as a 3D noise: raw vol is vertical extrusions. It works only as h minus y density.
kernels: Value+gradient Perlin (perlin2 derivative / perlin3g) and Simplex (simplex2 / simplex3g): used by fractal-derivative, fractal-slope-aligned and the erosion base; the one piece of plumbing all three need
Elliptical-kernel simplex (ellipSimplex2/3 in t_fractal_slope_aligned.cpp): simplex corner loop with a symmetric matrix on the offsets, continuous for any stretch >= 1
Phacelle 3x3 stripe kernel (stripes() in t_erosion_filter.cpp): jittered cells, polynomial weight with cut 1.25, bounded-phase sincos, min(2L,1)/L normalisation
Fixed per-octave rotation matrix applied to position and accumulators (rotv in t_fractal_derivative.cpp)
families.question: Which terrain gully method?

families.answer:
Dendry (the prototyper's cut-down form) is the river tree, and I agree it is the only entry that answers the family question: at seeds 7 and 42 and windows 8 and 24 it is a connected irregular tree with twig tributaries, an isotropic FFT and no seams (my jump scan at seed 7: 0 true jumps, worst 0.006; check and speed re-run match: 2700 ns scalar, 54.5x Perlin). Nothing in the existing nodes sheet gets near it: Ridged and warped F2-F1 give webs whose lines cross and close cells, never a tree, so this is not a graph recipe. Call: ship, as a hero/bake node for heightmaps, not a building block.

Where I disagree with the prototyper:
1. The wide view was understated. At 96 cells across (seed 42, window 24) the baseline width proxy follows the low-frequency drift field, so half the frame is a white blob and the other half thin scribble. It does not merely "dissolve into texture", it has large fat/thin zones. I fixed that with a per-segment local normalisation (wmode=1): width from the segment's own 3x3 min/max of the control instead of the absolute height. The tree then covers the wide view evenly with local trunk/twig hierarchy, close view unchanged, 0 jumps, same cost. A first attempt that normalised by the sample's 5x5 window seamed at every cell edge (17 true jumps), which is a trap any port must avoid: anything that modulates a segment must be a property of the segment, not of the sample's cell.
2. fern-fold drainage does not "read as rivers up close". At seed 7 and at seed 42 window 48 it reads as lightning or frost at every scale: dense feathery branches at a fixed angle. It costs the same as dendry (2661 ns measured). The folded tributaries are a different aesthetic (veins, frost) and only earn a mode on the dendry node, if that.
3. catchment-rivers headline cost is misleading. With the listed params (Perlin control) it is 7243 ns, 145x Perlin; the 72.5x is the hash-control figure (3739 ns measured). The prototyper disclosed this in the artifacts field but not in the number. The hillshaded elevation is genuinely the best terrain texture in the family, but every seed shows straight trunk spokes meeting at star hubs, and the K sweep being indistinguishable plus the DrainageFrame discovery say the exact-area walkers are not what makes it look good. Showcase, not a node.
4. Stochastic descent: the comparison image shows real reduction of star hubs, but at seed 7 dendry still has several multi-arm junctions and crossings that close small diamonds. "Reduced, not gone" is accurate; "mostly dissolve" is generous.

Agreed without reservation: flow-network fails the question (one-way tree, bow-tie FFT, no warp setting between combed and marble), spill-level is dull and expensive, basin-tree is dendry level 0 and its V/U/Box valley profiles should be dendry members. Dendry 3D is straight rods (vol at seed 7 confirms) and there is no 4D, so GenTileable2D would break; that is the biggest open port problem after cost. Multi-scale trunks (rivers longer than 10-20 cells) remain unsolved by every entry.
families.proto_answer:
Dendry wins as the river tree, in a cut-down form I call dendry lite: 4 levels, a 3x3 segment window per level, 5x5 control points, and each child searching only 2x2 parent cells. It is the only entry that reads as an irregular river map on the sheet and still has no flow axis at the wide view. Evidence and limits follow.

WHY THE OTHERS LOSE
- flow-network fails the question. A plain lattice has one direction for every seed: coherence 0.131 at 48 cells, and at 77 cells 0.044 with line angles 98, 89 and 97 degrees. Warp 16 drops the number to 0.012 with no fixed angle, but by then the image is marble and agate ribbons, not rivers. The warp sweep shows nothing in between that works, and the metric alone would have misled me here.
- fern-fold as specified has the same problem as visible bands. Its province layout gives separate sprigs. It only becomes a river tree when grown off steepest-descent trunks, and that needs the same window as Dendry, so its cost advantage is gone: scalar 2688 ns against dendry's 2740 ns. It is denser and looks like frost or lightning at 19 cells.
- basin-tree is dendry level 0 with better valley profiles, so it merges into dendry.
- catchment-rivers makes the best terrain but a poor tree (see the relief section).

DENDRY LITE IS AFFORDABLE
- The 3x3 window thumb is near identical to the paper-style 5x5 window, at scalar 2740 ns against 9582 ns.
- The jump scanner finds 0 true jumps. The lab c0ratio of 3.01 is its probe saturating on thin lines. That is why I wrote the bisecting scanner.

TWO CHANGES MADE THE TREES READ AS RIVERS, AND BOTH APPLY TO ANY OF THEM
1. Control field: a valley term |noise| plus a strong low-frequency drift term, giving long trunks.
2. Stochastic descent: a per-cell hash mask picks which neighbours a cell may drain to. This visibly breaks up the star-shaped hubs that all the control-driven trees had. I judged this by eye on a few seeds; there is no metric for it.
A hash-only form of the control works for the tree mask. Its base looks boxy at the wide view, so terrain views should use Perlin or the user's source.

RELIEF IS A DIFFERENT ANSWER
Carving any tree into terrain gives decent but soft valleys, except fern, which goes cliffy with one dramatic canyon. The most convincing terrain is catchment-rivers elevation in a local trunk frame, and the cheaper drainage-frame discovery is close behind it. The K sweep (2 to 16) is nearly indistinguishable by eye, so the exact area, though correct (0 mismatches in 900 sites against brute force), is not what makes it look good.

REMAINING FLAWS
- Width follows control height, not real discharge, so wide views have thick and thin zones. These are mild in dendry and strong in fern.
- Hubs are reduced, not gone, and diagonal links occasionally cross.
- At 77 cells across 512 px every tree dissolves into dendritic texture. By eye the longest rivers are about 10-20 cells, and multi-scale trunks are unsolved.
- 3D is level 0 only: straight rods. There is no 4D (625 control evals).
- Cost is far over the 5x Perlin guideline, so this is a hero or bake node.

MEASUREMENT CAVEATS
- All speeds are scalar prototypes, inflated by per-sample std::map parameter reads by an amount I did not measure.
- All AVX2 figures are estimates. Nothing was ported.
- The early wide comparison used unequal cell counts. I caught that and re-rendered it. Coherence at 19 cells rose to 0.024-0.052 with the hash control, which overlaps warped flow-network, because at that view a single drift slope dominates. The line angle changes per seed, unlike the plain lattice, and at 77 cells it falls to 0.005-0.009.

Dendry was written from the idea entry's description of the method. Neither the paper nor the GPL reference code was fetched.
challenged: dendry-noise: 'the wide panel keeps branching everywhere, with regional thick and thin zones' understates it; at 96 cells (seed 42, window 24) the baseline is half white blob, half thin scribble because width tracks the drift field. Fixed by per-segment normalisation (wmode=1).
fern-fold: 'reading as rivers up close' failed; at seed 7 window 16 and seed 42 window 48 the drainage layout reads as lightning/frost at every scale.

catchment-rivers: scalar_vs_perlin 72.5 does not describe the listed params; with cmode=2 (as listed and as used for every terrain image) I measured 7243 ns, 144.7x Perlin. 3739 ns (75.9x) only with cmode=3.
stochastic descent: 'hubs mostly dissolve into confluences' is generous; seed 7 dendry still shows several star junctions and diamond crossings. 'Reduced, not gone' holds.

A naive local width normalisation that reads the sample's window seams (17 true jumps, worst 0.359): the prototyper's cap-by-window argument covers geometry but not any per-sample modulation, which a port must keep per segment.
kernels: trunkFrame: steepest-descent trunks with per-segment (along, across) frame and seam-free fade, used by fern-fold, catchment-rivers and the DrainageFrame discovery. 7x7 control, 5x5 segments.
ctrlField in rivers_common.h: valley control |noise| plus low-frequency drift, with Perlin and hash-only forms, used by all control-driven trees.
Stochastic descent: per-cell hash mask over the lowest-neighbour search, in trunkFrame and inline in dendry and basin.
Two-walker upstream area on the Scheidegger lattice, used by flow-network and catchment-rivers: exact, 0 mismatches in 900 sites.
Bisecting true-jump scanner for thin-line fields, where the lab c0ratio saturates. axis_coherence.py alongside: whole-image structure tensor coherence and line angle per seed.
families.question: Which river tree?

families.answer:
WHICH CRACK NODE: CellularEdge, a new node on the exact bisector pass. Its crack outputs are Levels (ShatterBSP cuts), hybrid Edge Width and Edge Depth, and site Colours. recursive-cut-noise is not the #1 crack node as proposed. It survives only as a Strata mode of TileSplit.

LEVEL 0, THE PROOF. Root sweep at seeds 1337 and 31337 (recursive-cut-noise/grid.png):
- No root gives one parallel family per seed.
- A square root shows the lattice.
- Only a Voronoi root is isotropic.
Rotated cuts cannot fix it, because level 0 has one id (the seed) and so one direction. I also tried the only rotation-based escape: hiding the first K levels so the first visible lines are rotated per strip. Ghost 1 still shows the aligned family, and ghost 2-3 turn to needle hatch that no longer reads as cracks.
So the Voronoi root is the fix. Once it is in, line families only add hatching at lac 1.3 and above (re-rendered with the fixed code at seed 4242) and cost 11.5x perlin scalar against 8.6x for single cuts. I agree with the prototyper's merge on that branch.

WHERE I DISAGREE WITH THE PROTOTYPER:
1. Root-free levels 3 is worth keeping. Parallel beds with joints that stop at them are clean, c0 7.98, with no window. It is a TileSplit mode, not a failure to discard.
2. The vertex jumps are solved, in two ways, so Edge Drop and the per-wall hash go.
   - Site colours with d = max( e, kd * ( F_other - F1 ) ): c0 8.00, 0 jumps above 0.2 in 3M 2D and 800k 3D samples at kd 0.2 or more.
   - A smooth strength sampled at the sample, driving width and depth together: c0 7.66-7.93, and the tips narrow as they fade.
3. Make it a new node, not CellularDistance return types, because Size Jitter and non-Euclidean metrics would sit there invalid.
4. T-junctions and bricks do not by themselves justify nodes. Both can be built from existing nodes (see below).
I also reject the earlier critic's ContourCut as the answer. Its relief is good, but thin closed rings appear around lattice vertices at seeds 31337 and 4242, and the 32-unit view is a meandering scribble.

JITTER CAP: default GridJitter 0.90, range up to 1.0. My own max-min search gives the exact limit below which a 3^D window is correct:
- 2D: r* 0.4106-0.4114 (GJ 0.940)
- 3D: r* 0.3629-0.3637 (GJ 0.917)
- 4D: r* 0.3324-0.3331 (GJ 0.909)
These are search results, not proofs, and they agree with the earlier hill climb. The prototyper's ring 0.40 is safe in 2D only, and its claim that 3D is exact at the default 0.396 is false.
- Worst error at GJ 1.0: 0.0327 / 0.0358 / 0.0409.
- Real FastNoise generator at GJ 1.0: 2D 149 of 12M wrong (max 0.0245), 3D 0 of 1.5M, 4D 0 of 200k.
- GJ 0.95 and below in 2D: 0 of 12M.
- Masks of half width 0.10 or less at GJ 1.0: 0 wrong in 12M.
- The worst real seam is a kink deep in one cell, visible only in shading.
0.90 and 1.0 look the same. The same-window pass is better than F1-centred (t_edge_audit reproduced exactly).

GRAPH FINDINGS (measured with fnlab on base.dll):
- Three-level T-junction cracks from existing nodes: per-cell DomainOffset of the child network. 35 / 106 / 345 ns AVX2, check 0 FAIL at scale 8. True T-junctions, but the F2-F1 walls stay fat, and it is 3x or more the estimated node cost.
- Running-bond brick wall with per-brick tone: 16 / 46 / 148 ns, but AVX512 parity FAIL on 27% of samples.
- Tapered cracks: 7 / 18 / 50 ns, with black wedges and dotted hairlines.

BIGGEST NEW RESULT: simplex-window Voronoi, 6 / 8 / 10 sites instead of 9 / 27 / 81.
- Scalar 3D 309 ns against 871 ns; 2D 269 ns against 364 ns.
- At rings 0.28 / 0.17 / 0.14, F1 and clamped masks had 0 wrong in 1.5M / 300k / 40k samples, and 0 jumps in 2M 2D and 500k 3D samples.
- Only clamped masks are exact. Unclamped distance is wrong on 0.1-2.6% of samples at those rings, so wide bevels keep the square window.
- Sites are more regular, about half the default jitter in 3D. The nested 3D vol at ring 0.17 shows a near-honeycomb, while shards look fine.
- My estimate is about 5 / 7 / 10 ns AVX2 against the prototyper's 5.5 / 16 / 50.

NOT DONE: no node was ported, so every AVX2 figure for a new idea is an estimate. Simplex-window 4D is a geometry audit only, with no Eval4 render. I did not test tileable TileSplit.
families.proto_answer:
Which crack node: not recursive-cut-noise as proposed. The root sweep (12-unit window) proves that with no root, level 0 is one global family of parallel lines for the whole seed and every wide view is parallel strips with cross cuts; a square grid root swaps that for a visible lattice; only a Voronoi root is isotropic. With the Voronoi root the node is ShatterBSP with line families instead of single cuts, and the families bring their own flaw: at lacunarity >= 1.3 a family crosses an elongated sub-cell several times and hatches it (the lacunarity grid). At f=1, lac=1.15 with per-strip boundary jitter 0.5 it matches ShatterBSP almost pixel for pixel with occasional close parallel pairs, and it has lost its two selling points (no window, dimension-independent cost). So recursive-cut-noise is merged into shatter-bsp. The crack node to build is CellularShatter: Voronoi root from the CellularDistance window, exact edge distance, then Levels single BSP cuts through a tracked sub-cell centre (one cut per cell per level, T-junctions, hierarchical widths, C0 measured 8.0, leaf value / tilt / bevel outputs, 3D shards confirmed). Best at 3 levels, width decay 0.85; at 5-6 levels the cuts fan around the centre into slivers. Scalar 8.5x perlin2 with trig; estimate ~7 / 18 / 52 ns AVX2 (2D/3D/4D). Levels=0 is exactly CellularEdgeDistance, so the two can be one node.

Exact edge distance and the jitter cap: measured with t_edge_audit (640k 2D and 346k 3D samples per radius against a 5^D brute force). A second pass over the SAME stored 3^D window around the sample cell (zero extra hashes) is exact up to ring jitter 0.40 in 2D (0 wrong), 0.0003% wrong at the default 0.437 (max error 0.005 cell), 0.19% at 0.50; in 3D it is exact at the default 0.396 and 0.005% wrong at 0.45. The F1-centred 3^D second pass used by earlier audits is worse (0.84% wrong at 0.437 in 2D) and costs 3^D-1 extra hashes, because the bisectors that matter lie near the sample, not near F1. Decision: no jitter change at FastNoise defaults, cap at 0.40 if strict exactness is wanted, and never re-centre the window. CellularEdgeDistance is a keeper (c0 8.0, constant-width EdgeMask vs the fat-at-junction F2-F1, facet relief, polyhedra vol); ship it as CellularDistance return types or as a CellularEdge node that also carries the edge-fate outputs: Pebble (C0, convincing cobbles and 3D gravel), Plate, Crack with Edge Drop (dangling mud cracks, but jumps up to the crack depth in notches at vertices, c0 1.04, unsolved), Crease (nested cracks with T-junctions from a terraced region source, same vertex jumps). Per-edge width alone is C0. Cellular-fracture rays were weak (scratches); its order-2 sector value is a nice free output. TileSplit is a separate keeper: window-free bonds (grid, running, basket, herringbone) plus KD splits, exact box distance, per-tile wood interior, 2.1x perlin scalar, 3D brick wall; it absorbs recursive-cut's axis-aligned grid-root mode. Crystal-grains reserve works (rotated hex-pyramid grains, zoned concentric hexagons, c0 8.0) but had only 3 iterations: promising, not a crack node.
challenged: Prototyper: 3D edge distance exact at the default ring 0.396, so no jitter change is needed. My search finds failures above r* 0.3629-0.3637 (GJ 0.917), worst error 0.0358. The real generator showed 0 of 1.5M, so this is true only as a sampling result.

Prototyper: 2D max error 0.005 at the default ring. Worst case is 0.0327 by search and 0.0245 on the real generator over 12M independent samples. t_edge_audit does reproduce 0.0053, but it samples 4 seeds on a contiguous block.

Prototyper: Edge Drop and Crease vertex jumps are unsolved and a continuous drop needs all window pairs. Site colours with F_other need one compare per stored site and give c0 8.00 with 0 jumps above 0.2 in 3M 2D and 800k 3D samples (kd 0.2 or more, GridJitter 0.90).
Prototyper: Voronoi-root recursive cut matches ShatterBSP almost pixel for pixel. The comparison shows the same style, but the interior cuts do not coincide.

Prototyper: Order-2 kite mosaic is something no existing value mode produces. Add of CellularValue index 0 and 1 gives the same kind of partition (25 / 78 / 255 ns AVX2), with different walls and correlated tones.
Prototyper evidence: the lacunarity grid predates the strip-pick fix (file 01:44:33, fix logged 01:47:16). The hatching conclusion still holds on a re-render at seed 4242.

Catalogue and earlier critic: T-junctions cannot come from a graph, and Min of two F2-F1 only crosses. A per-cell DomainOffset makes the child network stop at the parent wall. Three levels pass check with 0 FAIL at 35 / 106 / 345 ns.

Earlier critic: nothing in the existing nodes gives bricks with a per-tile id. A graph makes a running-bond wall with tone and mortar at 16 / 46 / 148 ns, though it fails AVX512 parity on 27% of samples.

Earlier critic: recursive-cut-noise should ship as ContourCut. Thin closed rings appear around lattice vertices at seeds 31337 and 4242, and the 32-unit view is a scribble rather than a crack network.
kernels: Templated 3^D Voronoi pass (F1/F2, stored sites and hashes) plus the exact bisector second pass over the SAME window (pass2=0) or F1-centred (pass2=1) and a 5^D brute-force reference; used by t_cellular_edge_distance, t_shatter_bsp, t_edge_fate_cells, t_recursive_cut_noise (Voronoi root)
Jitter-radius audit of the edge distance (same-window exact to ring 0.40 2D / 0.396 3D; F1-centred window is worse)
Symmetric per-edge hash mix(ha ^ hb, ha + hb) for per-wall attributes (edge-fate, crease, order-2 value)
BSP descent with decreasing depth per level (max over levels stays C0) shared by shatter-bsp, recursive-cut and tile-split crack modes
families.question: Which crack node?

families.answer:
WHICH CAVE BASE. I agree with the prototyper on the shape of the answer and disagree on two supporting claims.

For spaghetti tunnels: TubeNoise in Network mode on Perlin + value-term channels. I re-rendered tube and net3 at a fresh seed (42) and a wider window (8), and rendered the real abs+abs graph through fnlab at the same air fraction and seed. The classic recipe is flanged ribbon-sheets every time; tube and network are round-section worms every time. That is not a cherry-picked seed. The cost is real: plain Tube is separate closed loops (prototyper table 37% largest air component at 5% air, which I did not re-measure), there are flat lens flakes in every render, and 4D is 10.3x perlin2 scalar (527 ns), so tileable 2D will be slow.

For a connected labyrinth: the gyroid, but note what the table actually measured. The caves table's "gyroid warped" rows are a=4 wf=.1 and a=3 wf=.1 oct2, and in the prototyper's own cave sheet those are a honeycomb crystal. The organic bone net the text recommends is a=6.6 oct2, which was not in the table. At seed 42 window 8 that cut (iso 0.887 at per=1.5) is a good foam skeleton with three-way junctions, the best connected-cave image in the family.

DOES TUBE-NOISE FIX PINCHING? The prototyper's own answer is the right one: the plain recipes do not pinch closed, they flange. Tube fixes the flanging (verified by eye at two seeds against the real graph; the measured CVs are the prototyper's, not re-measured). It does not fix connectivity; network mode does, partly.

DOES HYBRID PHASE + WARP BREAK GYROID PERIODICITY? Translation order yes above about 3 rad; orientation order no. At window 12 (seeds 3, 7, 42) the sponge is a polycrystal of parallel-channel domains, and the window-16 FFT keeps its axis cross at axis 16-19 for oct=2, not the 10 reported. I tried two fixes: a bigger slower warp (a=10, wf=.12) keeps the grain, and a noise-weighted blend of two gyroid frames (my mutation, mixf param) adds diagonal spokes to the FFT instead of removing the cross (axis 18.8 vs 19.1). Bounded warp cannot remove orientation order because its Jacobian stays near 1; what survives is connectivity and smoothness, which is still worth having.

Where I disagree most: TPMS uniqueness. I built the plain gyroid from existing nodes in fnlab (3 SineWave + 3 DomainOffset + 3 RemoveDimension + 2 Add, period 2, 3.69 ns AVX2 3D) and the warp is just DomainWarpGradient on that graph. Every other family is the same kind of trig sum. So TPMSNoise is a convenience node with about a 2x speed win, not a new look; I still say ship it because nobody will assemble an 11-node graph for a gyroid, but without the built-in warp.

Scalar/AVX2 anchors I measured: tube 3D 99 ns (2.01x perlin2), net3 118 ns, tube 4D 527 ns; TPMS plain 42 ns (0.83x), TPMS a=6.6 oct2 298 ns (5.83x perlin2, so the 9 ns AVX2 estimate for the warped form is the low end); real abs+abs graph AVX2 2.60/5.16/7.39 ns (prior critic bench, matches the 5.25 claim); gyroid graph 3.86/3.69/4.87 ns.
families.proto_answer:
WHICH CAVE BASE. There are two winners, for different caves, and the classic recipe is neither.

For spaghetti worm tunnels, use TubeNoise in network mode, built on Perlin channels with a per-vertex value term. For a guaranteed connected labyrinth or sponge, use a warped gyroid (TPMSNoise).

The numbers below use equal air fraction and about 0.8 air pockets per unit^2 of slice, so feature size is comparable:

| Base | 5% air: section CV | 5% air: largest air component | 12% air: section CV | 12% air: largest air component |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| abs+abs (two Simplex) | .406 | 93% | .405 | 99% |
| Tube | .281 | 37% | .293 | 71% |
| Tube network | .285 | 77% | .312 | 86% |
| Gyroid, warped | .306 | 100% | .299 | 100% |

Section CV here is the local-thickness coefficient of variation. One-sided Simplex at 5% air has a largest component of only 1%, so it makes pockets rather than tunnels.

How they look:
- abs+abs is flanged, webbed ribbons.
- Tube is clean separate worms.
- Tube network is a dense tangle.
- Warped gyroid is a bone or foam skeleton with three-way junctions.

Measured AVX2 cost of the abs+abs graph in 3D is 5.25 ns. Estimated port costs in 3D are 4.5-6.5 ns for tube, 5-7.5 ns for network, and 1.9 ns for plain gyroid, rising to 5.5-9 ns with warp.

DOES TUBE-NOISE FIX PINCHING? Yes for shape, with a real connectivity cost.

The plain recipes do not really pinch closed. At 5% air, no section fell below a third of the median radius in any recipe. Their actual failure is flanges and blowouts.

On the same simplex channels at 5% air, tube compares with abs+abs like this:
- Radius CV: .125 vs .354.
- Section aspect: 1.29 vs 2.40.
- Radius p05/median: .97 vs .66.
- Blowouts: 2.5% vs 20.7%.
- Air more than 2x the median radius from any centre line: 0.3% vs 9.7%.

Length is no rounder than abs+abs or Max (.359 / .354 / .358), so that claim in the vector-simplex entry is false.

The cost is that those webs were what connected the recipes. Largest air component drops from 92% to 42% because true tubes are separate closed loops. Network mode (3 channels, min over pairs, real junctions where all three vanish) restores 95% on those channels and 90% on Perlin + value. Its radius CV is about .25 because junctions count as wide sections.

Radius holds from about 0.05 to 0.2 feature units and merges into blobs at 0.35. Damping should stay small: L=.02 on Perlin gave CV .132, L=.5 gave .239.

One flaw not in the entries: every gradient channel on one lattice is exactly zero at every vertex, because kernel r^2 is below the vertex edge^2. The tubes therefore thread the lattice.
- 2D Perlin shows a visible integer grid of dots.
- Simplex shows big blobs where kernels leave gaps.
- Pierce density is 11.73 vs 6.06 per unit^2.

A per-vertex value term from spare hash bits fixes this on Perlin at one lattice. Tube radius CV is .132 vs .130 for two lattices, and the grid is gone. Simplex still blobs noticeably in the Length form. Hence vector-simplex-length is merged: the speed is real (scalar 1.11x one simplex against 1.74x for two), but it has no look of its own.

DOES HYBRID PHASE + WARP BREAK GYROID PERIODICITY? Translation order yes, orientation order only partly, and only above a threshold amplitude.

Autocorrelation at one period is 1.0 plain, .68 at 1 rad, .20 at 2 rad, and 0 at 4 rad. With a fast warp it stays flat out to 8 periods, because bounded warp leaves a constant periodic residue. 1.5-3 rad still reads as a bent lattice in the vol views.

A slow large warp is the regime that works. Perlin a=6.6, wf=.157 gives ac(P) .15, ac(2P) 0, solid 3 components, void 2, and a smooth sponge with no visible repeat in a 12 unit window. Fast warp shreds it: Simplex a=4, wf=.5 gives 258 and 213 components.

Honest limits:
- The FFT keeps an axis cross. Axis stat at window 16 is 45 plain, 37 one octave, 10 two octaves.
- Wall uniformity largely goes. Local thickness CV is .232 plain, .29-.335 warped, and about .345 for thresholded Perlin at iso 0.
- What survives is connectivity and smoothness: 1-4 components against 12-44 for plain noise at iso 0, and visibly rounder saddle walls.

Warp with Perlin, not Simplex. Simplex 3D's r2=.6 jumps get amplified (c0ratio 4.2 vs 8.0). A one-lattice 3-channel warp measures the same as three separate noises, so an in-node warp is worth it.

All numbers are scalar prototype measurements or measured fnlab anchors, and AVX2 figures for new nodes are estimates. No real node was built, so tiling and SIMD parity are untested beyond looking at torus-mapped prototypes.
challenged: TPMS FFT axis stat 'at window 16 ... 10 two octaves': my window-16 sheets read 16.05 (seed 7, prior critic image) and 19.14 (seed 42) for a=6.6 wf=.157 oct=2; the two-octave warp does not weaken the cross versus one octave.

The caves comparison table's 'Gyroid, warped' rows (a=4 wf=.1 and a=3 wf=.1 oct2) are a visible honeycomb crystal in the prototyper's own cave sheet, so the 100% connectivity / CV .306 figures describe a crystal lattice, not the organic a=6.6 sponge the text recommends, which was never in the table.

'A smooth sponge with no visible repeat in a 12 unit window' for a=6.6 wf=.157: window-12 vol views at seeds 3, 7 and 42 show domains of locally parallel channels (polycrystal). No exact repeat, but orientation order is plainly visible.
TPMS '3D with one-lattice warp is 2.55x' describes oct=1; the recommended oct=2 preset measures 5.83x perlin2 scalar (298 ns) in my run, and the AVX2 estimate of about 9 ns is the low end.

TubeNoise estimated 4D AVX2 7-12 ns: scalar 4D is 10.3x perlin2 (527 ns) with 16 lattice corners and 2-3 channels of Jacobian, so my estimate is 20-40 ns (estimate, not measured); GenTileable2D will be slow.

Plain gyroid has no cheap existing-node form (implied by 'TPMSNoise ... no lattice' as a new primitive): a verified 11-node graph of SineWave + DomainOffset + RemoveDimension + Add renders an exact gyroid at 3.69 ns AVX2 3D, and DomainWarpGradient on it gives the warped sponge.
kernels: One-lattice multi-channel gradient noise with a per-vertex value term, Simplex and Perlin, 2D to 4D, with analytic Jacobian: t_tubes_common.h vecSimplex and vecPerlin. Used by TubeNoise, its Length/MaxAbs outputs and the TPMS warp.
Levenberg-damped Gauss-Newton distance for 1 to 3 channels: t_tubes_common.h gnDistance.
TPMS field set with warp hooks.
Measurement tool for cave comparisons (equal air and pocket density, cross-section radius, false air, connected components, local thickness, lattice-lag autocorrelation).
families.question: Which cave base?

families.answer:
Which network: bond-tunnels in Percolation mode, p about 0.6, is the one to build from this family, but as the structured network node, not as the default cave, and none of the family is strictly connected by construction.

Connectivity on seeds the prototyper did not use (99, 2024, plus 7 where stated):
- Bond p=0.6: 97.7-98.5% in a 6^3 box, 100.00% in the core of an 11^3 box (cave voxels at least 3 cells from the wall). The missing share in the box is branches the box cuts, so the reported 99.1-99.6% was the wrong measure. p=0.5 gives 100.00 and 97.00% in the core, p=0.45 97.5 and 97.9%, p=0.4 95.3% with 13 sealed pockets. The usable floor is about p=0.5.
- Truchet: the prototyper's 55 components, largest 3.5%, is false. NETCONN ran at static init before the pairing table was filled, so it measured parallel x cylinders. Real figures: 99.1-99.3% in 6^3 and 100.00% in the core, at 21-22% void. It connects only because fat tubes overlap: r .1-.17 gives 9.0% in the box and 9.59% in the core, so the 'never branch' half of the claim holds.
- Spanning: tree mode is a forest, 54.62% even in the core. Bond-graph mode p=0.5 is 95.3-96.6% in 6^3, not the reported 98.1%, and 98.54-100.00% in the core.
- Strata is the only member with walkable floors: 97.4-100% in 6^3 and 100.00% in the core of 12^3 on 3 seeds. It is a different axis, not a tube network.

Where I disagree with the prototyper's pick: 'the only member connected and cheap' fails against existing nodes.
- Add(Multiply(a,a), Multiply(b,b)) of two real Perlin nodes is 99.99-100.00% in the core at 11% void, 9.29 ns AVX2 measured, needs no warp, has no lattice, and looks more organic, though with flanged webs.
- Real CellularDistance F3-F1 is 99.99% at 11% void on seed 99, 12.2-12.7 ns, and looks like faceted struts.
- Bond measured 9.31 ns in a direct AVX2 kernel, so the 8-10 ns estimate holds, but bond plus warp is 12.92 ns (9.31 + 3.61, sum of two measurements).
- Bond's exclusive ground is the unwarped corridor maze and plumbing, chambers and dead ends, and connection at very low void: 100.00% in the core at 2.5% void and 99.27% at 1.4%. There the noodle graph is at 0.13-6.43% and F3-F1 at 0.00% at 2.5%.
- Its 4D form is useless: through the 4D torus that GenTileable2D uses it is isolated dots, measured on bond. Any line network has this geometry.

How much warp hides the lattice:
- Rotation alone hides nothing: k=1 peak/median 4388 vs 4191.
- The prototyper's 0.3@1.2 + 1.2@0.2 does not 'remove all straight lines': on seed 99 a grid still reads at windows 8 and 14, peak 209-266.
- Its amplitudes are in prototype Perlin units and do not transfer. The real DomainWarpGradient is hermite value noise with RMS 0.39 x amplitude, against 0.22 x for the prototype Perlin. Real warp nodes on a real regular lattice (F3-F1, Grid Jitter 0) left peak 78566 at amp 0.66 cells FS 5 cells and 639 with a warped grid still legible at 0.9 cells FS 3.3 cells. It fell to 58 only at 1.25 cells FS 1.7 cells.
- For bond through a scalar replica of that warp node, my recommendation is DomainRotate plus 2-octave DomainWarpFractalProgressive (Lacunarity 4, Gain 0.12) over DomainWarpGradient with amplitude about 1 cell and Feature Scale about 1.7 cells. That is about 0.4 cell RMS, chosen as a balance. The grid no longer reads at window 8 (seed 99), or at 0.9 cells at window 14 (seed 2024), and peak is 261-348. It stays above the 136 at 1.25 cells and the 41 at 1.6 cells FS 2 cells, where tubes shear visibly into flakes.
- Short range order tracks amp x freq, long range order tracks RMS. Warp costs connectivity: 98.16-99.93% in the core at 1 cell, 96.21-99.87% at 1.25 cells, 86.65% for thin tubes at 1 cell (voxel limited at 16 voxels per cell).
- Warped, bond and spanning cannot be told apart, and Truchet differs mainly by void.
- Strata does want a warp, contrary to the report, but a y-only one. It keeps floors flat, varies layer thickness and tilts the beds, and is the best image in the family. A y warp and dip added to the graph recipe gets close at 33.92 ns, so strata is a preset, not a node.

Limits of this pass:
- Bond is not a real node, so real warp on bond is through the replica. Real warp nodes ran only on the F3-F1 lattice.
- Truchet and spanning AVX2 costs are still estimates.
- The 4D torus was run only on bond.
- A previous critic pass had already written files here, including overwriting gallery images. I treated them as unverified. I agree with it on the Truchet bug, the spanning merge, the strata call and the hybrid seam. I differ on its Perlin-unit warp recipe and on its box-only p figures, and it did not test the a^2+b^2 graph.
- Prototype edits: t_networks_common.h (rw, core), t_bond_tunnels.cpp (mode 3, coarse), t_strata_caverns.cpp (dip, ya, w3). Copies are *.prev2.* and t_strata_caverns.prev.cpp.
families.proto_answer: Which connected-by-construction cave network: bond-tunnels in Percolation mode (p about 0.6, with a hub chamber) is the one to build. It is the only member that is both connected IN VIEW and cheap: a voxel flood fill of a 6^3-cell box put 99.1-99.6% of the cave in one component (23-26 components, the rest tiny orphan stubs, 0 sealed pockets), from a one-cell window (7 hashes, 12 segment distances in 3D; measured scalar 2.5x perlin2 in 2D, estimate 8-10 ns AVX2 3D). Truchet-noise is NOT a connected network despite the promise: its tubes never branch or meet, so the same box held 55 separate strands with the largest holding 3.5% of the cave (49 with fat tubes, 53 with straight pairings); it is a good 2D pattern node (1.1x perlin) but fails as a cave. Spanning-tunnels gives the same topology family as bond-tunnels (tree mode: 67 vs 73 components in the box, bond-graph mode p=0.5: 98.1% connected) at a 3^n window and 6.3x perlin scalar in 2D, so it is merged into bond-tunnels as the Link enum {Percolation, Tree, Both}; the "one spanning tree" guarantee is only asymptotic and any finite view shows many separate trees, which makes Tree mode the worst choice for a playable cave. Strata-caverns is a keeper on a different axis: not a tube network but stacked flat-floored galleries with domed ceilings and vertical shafts, 98.6% connected with S=1.5, ps=0.9, cov=0.25, a look nothing on the existing sheet or in this family produces; it costs one plan source eval plus 4 masked shaft evals. How much warp hides the lattice: a rotation alone removes axis alignment but the regular knot spacing still reads as a grid; a single fine warp of 0.3 cells at frequency 1.2 bends tubes and removes right angles in 2D while straight runs remain in 3D; two octaves (0.3 at 1.2 plus 1.2 at 0.2, after DomainRotate) remove all straight lines and give a woven root or vessel mass, at which point bond-tunnels and spanning-tunnels are indistinguishable; 0.5 at 1.2 starts to pinch tubes. Warping did not break connectivity (99.6% at 8^3, one pinched voxel pocket). Even fully warped, a uniform weave density remains visible because every cell has a hub; that is the residual lattice signature and a hybrid Bond Chance driven by a low-frequency noise is the obvious next step to break it. Strata-caverns does not need a warp (floors must stay flat; in-plane warp 0.4 barely changed the look).
challenged: Truchet is not a connected network (55 components, largest 3.5%): measurement bug, NETCONN ran at static init before gMatchInit and flood filled parallel x cylinders. Re-measured 99.1-99.3% in 6^3 on seeds 99 and 2024, 100.00% in the 11^3 core at 21-22% void. Only thin tubes are disconnected (rmax <= 0.17: 9%).

Bond is the only member connected in view and cheap: real Add(a^2, b^2) of two Perlin is 99.99-100.00% in the core at 11% void, 9.29 ns AVX2, no warp. Real F3-F1 is 99.99% at 11% void, 12.2-12.7 ns. Bond plus warp is 12.92 ns. Bond wins only below about 5% void or in its unwarped rectilinear look.

Bond 99.1-99.6% in one component: on unseen seeds 97.7-98.5% in 6^3. That number mostly measures box cuts; the 11^3 core is 100.00%, so the claim is low on the true figure and high on its own measure.
Connected by construction: bond is statistical (p=0.4 95.3% in the core with 13 sealed pockets). My mode 3 spine rule, which is connected by construction, did worse in view than p=0.6.
Two octaves (0.3@1.2 + 1.2@0.2) remove all straight lines: seed 99 still reads as a grid at windows 8 and 14, k=1 peak/median 209-266.

Warp amounts as stated transfer to the real graph: real DomainWarpGradient is hermite value noise (RMS 0.39 x amp vs 0.22 x for proto Perlin). On a real lattice with real warp nodes, 0.66 cells FS 5 cells leaves peak 78566 and a clear grid.

Warping did not break connectivity: with the real warp replica, core 98.16-99.93% at 1 cell, 96.21-99.87% at 1.25 cells, thin tubes 86.65% at 1 cell (voxel limited), and sealed pockets appear (31-46 at 1 cell).

A hybrid Bond Chance is the obvious next step: sampled at the point it gives c0ratio 1.03, max slope 1851 (tubes cut with a jump). Face centre sampling is continuous but costs 2n source evals. A low frequency mask in a graph on top does the job instead.
4D is the same loop over 8 faces: run through a 4D torus as GenTileable2D does, it is isolated dots, and a flat 3D slice is fragments. No tiling and no w animation.
Spanning bond-graph p=0.5 98.1%: 95.3-96.6% in 6^3 on seeds 99 and 2024.

Strata is a look nothing else produces: the existing-node graph gives the same floors, domes, plans and shafts on my seeds at 32.06 ns (33.92 with y warp and dip), though 40 nodes and with blind shaft ends.

Strata does not need a warp: a y-only warp keeps floors flat, varies layer thickness and removes the ruler; a y-only dip tilts the beds. Clearly better image, connectivity unchanged (99.98-100.00% in the core).
Strata defaults 76.7% and pillar setting 52.8%: 51.1% and 35.3% in 6^3 on seed 99.

Scalar ratios: bond 2.52x was the tree default; 7.13x perlin2 under the harness with the recommended params. Strata 18.92x, not 9.77x. These run through the parameter map, so they overstate; the measured AVX2 ratio for bond is 4.2x Perlin 3D.
kernels: segDist (point-segment), smin (polynomial smooth min), warp2/warp3 and domain2/domain3 (fixed rotation + two-octave perlin domain warp pre-pass used for the lattice-hiding comparison), finish (inv sign flip for pipes-vs-cave vol views), NETCONN voxel flood-fill connectivity test (env NETCONN="N,L,iso[,k=v...]": cave fraction, component count, largest component share, sealed pockets)

Face-hash seam rule shared by truchet-noise and bond-tunnels: hash a face by its lower cell + axis so both cells agree, and clamp the signed distance at a dmax below which only that face's own tube can be seen from face points (truchet: dmax <= 0.5 - rmax; bond: dmax <= min(stub, 0.5 - jitter - rmax) - smooth)

Window lemma shared by spanning-tunnels and the bond-graph reserve: with point jitter J <= 0.25 any bond with an endpoint outside the 3^n window is >= 0.5 - J from the sample cell, so clamping at dmax = 0.5 - J - rmax makes the clamped min exact
Percolation / tree link rule (same hash scheme in bond-tunnels and spanning-tunnels): parentAxis(cellHash) with optional vertical bias; percolation via per-face hash < p

families.answer:
Which cheap warp: the 1D noise shear chain with the perpendicular pairs table, as one DomainWarp node (Kernel Noise/Parabola, Direction Pairs/Periodic3), is the only member of this family worth its own warp node, and it is not cheap. I re-benched the real nodes and they match the prototyper (AVX2 2D/3D/4D: DomainWarpGradient 0.93/1.76/3.47, progressive 3 over it 3.06/5.14/10.22, Perlin 0.90/2.12/4.10 ns). The chain's 6 ns warp-only 2D figure is the prototyper's AVX2 estimate, which I did not reproduce; taken at face value it is twice the cost of progressive Gradient 3 in 2D and only wins from 3D up. Its case is quality, not price: at equal rms displacement the Gradient replica folds into plateaus, rectangles and terraces (visible in the warped FBm, relief and equal area checker sheets) while the chain keeps even fibres and equal cell areas, and a 6 octave progressive Simplex graph gives crinkled foil and fold rings, not combed smoke. So yes, det=1 is visibly better than DomainWarpGradient at amplitude 1 and up, and the look is not reachable from existing nodes.

Plaid at low octaves: on an FBm source the chain shows a fine crosshatch at 2 steps and is clean from 3 (re-rendered at seed 21). The parabola and sine kernels are quasi periodic: on stripes at window 64 the parabola chain is a regular textile, wallpaper in the wide view, so Parabola is a documented cheap option for FBm-like sources only and Sine should not exist. The stretch field (lyapunov) is where plaid really lives: at seed 21 window 12 its wide view is a woven basket (axis 25) and every variant I tried kept a hatch, because the stretch of a 1D shear is constant along lines and the two strongest directions always show.

Seed variety: confirmed both ways. Without rotating the direction table seeds 1 to 3 share one grain direction; with rotation the seeds differ in layout (seed 21 and 7 both fine).

Where I disagree with the prototyper: (1) 'rising strain removes straight bands' is half true, it removes the straight lines but leaves a herringbone hatch at wide view, and the headline seed 1337 hides it best; I still call lyapunov-stretch ship because at the feature scale the hatch is the fibre direction a fur or brushed material wants, but clean is 4 not 7. (2) Periodic3 at 21 steps aliases at other seeds (seed 7: c0ratio 1.5, max slope 733); 9 steps is the usable setting (c0ratio 6.0). (3) The 3D volume of the 1D kernel is torn lamellar sheets, a real weakness the report understates; the noise2 option from Feistel should be the 3D default. (4) The hybrid noise then parabola chain is not a cost win worth having: on stripes the parabola tail still reads as a regular zigzag. (5) stretch-ftle curl worms are the most unique image in the family (nothing in the catalogue makes them) but at 632 ns scalar (12.3x perlin2), c0ratio 5.3 and a port that needs a built in Perlin Hessian per step, it is a showcase, not a node. Feistel is correctly folded into the shear node. I did not verify the 4D det and tile claims (no proto in the list) or the AVX2 kernel estimates.
families.proto_answer:
Build one shear chain node with a Noise kernel (the default) and a Parabola kernel (the speed option), and use a perpendicular pairs direction table. Noise 6 steps is the best quality per cost. Parabola 8 steps is the cheapest good warp. True sine and Feistel have no reason to exist as separate nodes.

**Cost.** Chain numbers are estimates from hand written AVX2 kernels, warp only, fixed seed, not FastSIMD. They are ns per sample, 2D/3D/4D.

| Warp | ns (2D/3D/4D) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Parabola, 8 steps | 3.3/3.9/4.4 | estimate |
| Noise, 6 steps | 6.1/6.5/7.1 | estimate |
| True sine, 8 steps | 7.9/8.9/9.7 | estimate |
| DomainWarpGradient | 0.94/1.76/3.43 | real node, Constant source |
| Gradient progressive, 3 octaves | 3.07/5.18/10.25 | real node, Constant source |
| DomainWarpSimplex | 1.67/4.75/10.52 | real node, Constant source |
| Simplex progressive, 3 octaves | 5.10/16.07/31.54 | real node, Constant source |

- The chains are not orders of magnitude cheaper, as the ideas claimed. They are latency bound, because each step feeds the next.
- A noise step costs about 1.0 to 1.15 ns, close to a full 2D Perlin sample (0.93), not the claimed one third.
- FS::Sin costs about 1 ns per step in a chain. The idea's 3 ns for 8 octaves holds only with my parabolic wave and before Source.
- Single octave Gradient stays cheapest. The chains match or beat progressive warps from 3D or 4D up, because their cost is nearly flat across dimensions.

**Plaid at low octaves.** On an FBm source, both chain kernels show straight bands at 1 step and a crosshatch at 2, gone by 3.

Regular sources are different for the sine and parabola kernels:
- Warped stripes at 4 octaves are practically the same image at a lag of (-97.25, 71.75), and the wide view is wallpaper.
- 8 and 16 octaves still read as a regular textile.
- Stretch field autocorrelation beyond 16 units: sine oct3 0.998, oct4 0.987, oct6 0.68, oct8 0.36, parabola oct16 0.12. The noise kernel gives 4 steps 0.25, 6 steps 0.11, 8 steps 0.08.

The sine and parabola repeat is why Noise is the default. The noise kernel has its own flaw at lac 1: long straight fault lines on stripes. Lacunarity of 1.3 or more reduced them. Gradient shows lattice locked pillow cells at every octave count from 1 to 5.

**Seed variety.** Phases alone are not enough:
- Without rotating the direction table per seed, 24 consecutive seeds share one grain direction (concentration 0.93 to 0.98).
- With rotation it falls to 0.01 to 0.21. Layouts then differ visibly across seeds in the contact sheets.
- Port cost of the rotation is not in the kernel numbers.

**Is det=1 visibly better than DomainWarpGradient?** Yes, in specific ways. At equal rms displacement of 1 unit, on a scalar replica of Gradient checked by eye against the real node:
- Gradient folds 15 percent of its area at 1 octave and 26 percent at 3 progressive octaves (det -2.2 to 7.4, and -11.8 to 41.9).
- It shows pillow plateaus and rectangular bands, and its relief has round lakes and terraces.
- The chains fold 0 percent, with det 1.000 within finite difference error in 2D, 3D and 4D.
- They show even fibres with no plateaus. Warped checker cells stay equal area, where Gradient makes big rectangles and slivers.

Part of the win is losing the lattice, not det=1:
- A control summing the same sine terms without chaining folds only 0.5 percent at rms 1 and looks fine.
- It folds 23 percent at rms 2, with crease knots appearing at amp 1.6, so det=1 is what holds at high amplitude.

Three claims did not hold up or need a caveat:
- Histogram and coverage preservation is not a selling point. KS distance is 0.002 to 0.011 for every warp, and coverage is 0.497 to 0.501.
- Golden direction tables add a global streak of their own (grain R 0.07 to 0.09 versus unwarped 0.007). The pairs table I found brings it to about 0.018 at the same cost.
- A fast varying hybrid amplitude breaks the guarantee: visible comb moire at +-100 percent, det sd 8.7.

**The rest of the family:**
- **LyapunovStretch** is a real new look, combed hair and feather barbs, once strain rises with frequency.
- **Analytic stretch** gives the same image as finite difference FTLE on a shear chain, at 2.8x less scalar cost.
- **FTLE on curl or gradient flows** gives different looks, curling worms and cell foam. It is promising but about 10 times the price, and belongs with a flow node.

**Method notes:**
- My first orientation histogram was not a plaid measure, because even unwarped Perlin peaks in the same diagonal bin. I replaced it with a structure tensor R.
- All FTLE AVX2 and Feistel AVX2 numbers are estimates with no kernel behind them.
challenged: lyapunov-stretch: 'rising strain removes the straight bands' - straight lines go but a herringbone/weave hatch remains in the wide view at seed 21 (axis 25, woven basket at window 48) and in every variant tried (golden table, gain 1.0/1.05, warm 2/3, 12 steps: axis 16 to 42); seed 1337 is the kindest seed

shear-flow: 'Periodic3 at 9 to 21 steps gives curling smoke, c0ratio 3.6' - at seed 7 with 21 steps c0ratio is 1.5 and max slope 733 (aliasing filaments); 9 steps gives c0ratio 6.0 with clean curls, so only 9 steps is usable

domain-warp-sine: 'Parabola 8 steps is the cheapest good warp' - on a stripe source at window 64 it is a regular textile with a wallpaper wide view; it is only good on FBm-like sources, and its 3.3 ns figure is an unverified estimate

shear-flow: the report presents 3D as working ('lamellar sheets') - the volume at seed 7 and the gallery vol are torn planar sheets from the 1D kernel, a visible 3D weakness that needs the noise2 option

family: 'chains match or beat progressive warps' - the only measured numbers are the real nodes (progressive Gradient 3 = 3.06 ns 2D); the chain costs are hand kernel estimates I could not reproduce, so the 2D cost comparison is unverified and on the estimates the chain is 2x dearer in 2D
kernels: Shear step p += u_k * (A_k / F_k) * f(F_k * dot(p, t_k) + o_k), det = 1 in any dimension, with exact inverse by reverse subtraction
Kernel f with derivative: 1D gradient noise (2 hashes, quintic) or parabolic wave t*(8 - 16*Abs(t))
Direction tables: perpendicular pairs with golden rotation between pairs (orthonormal frames in 3D and 4D), golden, periodic 3; all rotated per seed from a seed hash
Tangent vector propagation v += u * (A * f'(s) * dot(t, v)) with bounded output 1 - 2 * (1 + v.v)^-k
Hessian propagated Jacobian for flow FTLE on built in Perlin (perlin2h), no epsilon
families.question: Which cheap warp?

families.answer:
Which eddy warp: three small nodes, none shaped as reported.

(1) DomainWarpCurl with analytic potential, Steps (default 4) and Mode {Curl, Gradient}. Sub-stepping is the finding of this pass. One step is barely a new warp on bands; 4 steps give the hooks and eyes the report credited to 8-16 steps of DomainWarpFlow. Steps 4 and 12 look nearly the same on bands and Worley. At displacement 0.43 (seeds 2024, 555), det J spread is 2.13 / 0.59 / 0.19 at 1 / 4 / 12 steps and folded pixels are 28.6 / 0 / 0 %. Gradient mode from the same loop gives plates. Cost is unported: the real 45-node FD graph measures 24.96 / 44.78 / 72.08 ns AVX2, and analytic is estimated at about 6-8 ns 2D.

(2) DomainWarpFlow, reduced to Potential, Steps, Amplitude, Mode. It earns its place only where the potential matters. Jets plus oval storms in the potential are the family's only real Jupiter, with Kelvin-Helmholtz rollups and large spirals wrapped by the bands. Five of six seeds showed a large spiral, seed 7 only rollups, and it holds at window 24. DomainWarpSource is this node at Steps=1.

(3) A swirl node from VortexCells layers, with the 2x2 Impulse kernel as an overlap mode. On bands Impulse is the better picture and the cleaner one (c0 6.38 against 3.13). VortexCells keeps one site per layer at any dimension, against 4 / 8 / 16 per octave (arithmetic, not timed).

I disagree with merging vortex-cells and scatter-warp into curl: neither rotation kernel comes from a potential.

Pinching: gradient warps pinch bands into bubbles and crumple cells, as reported. But the independent warp does not avoid pinching: real DomainWarpGradient FS34 at the same displacement makes closed rings and islands on bands, and real Simplex and SuperSimplex make star junctions and dilated cushions on Worley.

Do curl warps look different from existing warps at the same amplitude?
- Single step on bands: no, you would struggle in a line-up. One step is not even area preserving at this strength: det spread 2.07 with 28% folded, against 1.45 and 24% for real Simplex at displacement 0.43.
- Single step on cells: yes. Cell area CV is 0.25 against 0.44-0.52 for real warps at 0.43.
- With 4 steps: clearly yes.
- Existing warps can fold: same-seed chains give plates with spiral eyes (13 nodes, 21.62 ns), and real shear stacks give even zigzag marble (43 nodes, 16.01 ns). Neither gives even marbling with hooks.

Jupiter ranking: jets plus storms, then jets alone, then VortexCells on waving bands (stamped), then SparseVortex (concentric rings). Marbling ranking on seeds 2024 and 555: curl or flow at 4-12 steps, then curl 3 octaves single step, then independent 3 octaves. I would not use any of these as a mountain terrain warp: fBm relief becomes streaked folds, and p99 slope rises with steps.

Limits of this pass:
- All port timings are estimates. Only real graphs and scalar prototypes were measured.
- I did not re-render the Push and Shear kernels, spiral sink or RK2, and did not compare Path Average with flow-strokes.
- Earlier look notes were written for images that had not actually displayed. The verdicts rest on images I then viewed plus measured numbers, but three cited images were not viewed in this pass, though the same parameters appear in panels I did view.
families.proto_answer: Which eddy warp: two nodes, not five. (1) DomainWarpCurl with an analytic Perlin potential is the cheap one (scalar 147 ns vs 219 ns for the independent-per-axis reference warp in the same harness; est. ~2/4/8 ns AVX2 per octave) and is the natural home for the sparse kernels: SparseVortex tangent push (identical picture to ScatterWarp's vortex kernel), exact-rotation discs (VortexCells / Impulse) and Sink. (2) DomainWarpFlow is the expensive one (scalar 17-32x perlin2; est. 20-50 ns 2D) and the only thing in the family that makes real ink marbling (8-16 steps along the rotated gradient fold ribbons over themselves) and watershed plates (descent with normalised, decaying steps gives flat-floored catchments whose borders are the ridge lines of the potential); it covers stir-advect and flow-watershed as modes. DomainWarpSource (FD of any node) is promising for generality, not for the promised fBm marbling: because every fBm octave contributes equally to the gradient, FD curl of a multi-octave potential is fine wrinkling, while a Cellular F1 potential gives a new faceted-shatter look (discovery). Pinching, measured at matched mean displacement 0.71 features: the gradient-of-potential warp pinches bands into bubbles and crumples cells into ridge nets; the independent-vector warp (what FastNoise's warps are) does not pinch but dilates and compresses regions, visible as cells of very unequal size on Worley and as large smooth patches next to tight folds at 3 octaves; curl keeps line density and cell size even everywhere. Do curl warps look different from existing warps at the same amplitude? Single warp on bands: barely, you would not pick it out of a line-up. On a cellular source: yes, cells stay the same size instead of some ballooning. With 3 progressive octaves: clearly yes, even marbling vs patchy marbling. Jupiter bands: the closest was VortexCells (exact disc rotations, density 0.4, 1.5 turns) chained after a gentle curl warp: oval eyes and teardrop storms on waving bands, but they read as stamped onto the bands rather than grown from the flow; SparseVortex at density 0.3-0.4 gives concentric target eyes in calm bands (first-order tangent push, so rings, not spirals). Marbling ranking from the images: Flow stir 12 steps > curl Perlin 3 octaves > independent 3 octaves > anything stamped. Scalar timings in this harness are dominated by param-map lookups and trig in rndDir2 (perlin2 itself reads 50 ns), so treat the ratios as rough; all AVX2 numbers are estimates.
challenged: DomainWarpFlow is the only thing in the family that makes real ink marbling and needs 8-16 steps: 4 analytic curl sub-steps give nearly the same picture as 12, seen on bands and Worley, seed 2024.
Existing warps never fold a ribbon over itself: same-seed real DomainWarpSimplex and DomainWarpGradient chains fold into plates with spiral eyes.

The independent-vector warp does not pinch: real DomainWarpGradient FS34 at matched displacement makes closed rings and islands on bands, and real Simplex and SuperSimplex make star junctions on Worley.

Curl keeps line density and cell size even everywhere: only partly. Cell area CV is lower than real warps, but a single step at displacement 0.71 folds 42.8% of pixels and has det spread 5.81. Evenness of that kind needs sub-steps.

Curl is much cheaper than the independent warp (147 vs 219 ns): this harness bias is large, the same warp reads 155-217 ns depending on how many keys are passed. At equal key count it is 180-189 vs 221-226 ns, about 1.2x.

Facet shatter: no existing node or graph can do it. Real FD curl of Euclidean F1 reproduces it closely at 12 nodes and 18.12 ns (wider breaks rather than thin tears), and a per-cell shift gives a straight-shard variant at 4 nodes and 21.10 ns.

Fluted cones are not available from existing warps: half true. Independent fractal warps give blobby cells, but a real 16-node FD curl graph at 21.21 ns gives the same star pits and fluted relief, so it is a recipe, not a reason for a node.

Normalise plus decaying step is required for descent and unnormalised speed overshoots into chaos: plain descent is clean at a step of 0.19 features, shows stripes at 0.25, grain at 0.38 and static from 0.5.
Sink is a kernel worth keeping: its foam is the same glass-crumple family as a progressive gradient warp, rounder and less lattice aligned, so Gradient mode covers it closely enough.

VortexCells is a fair Jupiter candidate and belongs in the curl node: on bands it reads as stamped, as the report admits, but its better use is layered fBm curls, and exact disc rotation does not come from a potential.
kernels: Potential with analytic gradient from one lattice visit (perlin2h / perlin3g; 3D curl = grad phi x grad psi of two potentials sharing hashes): DomainWarpCurl, reference warps, and the cheap path for DomainWarpFlow when the potential is left empty

Sparse 3^d jittered-site kernel window with smooth density gate and (1-r2)^n envelope: DomainWarpCurl SparseVortex == ScatterWarp vortex; Sink and Impulse/exact rotation are the same loop with a different per-site formula
Exact rotation (2D rotation matrix / Rodrigues about a hashed axis): VortexCells discs and the Impulse kernel
Forward-difference d+1 tap gradient of an arbitrary GeneratorSource at a moved position: DomainWarpSource and every step of DomainWarpFlow
Progressive-octave driver (DomainWarpFractalProgressive semantics: warp the already-warped position, amp *= gain, freq *= lac): used by every warp here, all of which fit the existing Warp() interface
Shared comparison harness (same bands/fBm/checker/Worley sources, reference indep/grad/curl warps scaled to mean displacement 0.71 at A=1, out=1 displacement-magnitude output for amplitude matching)

families.answer:
QuasiTile is the aperiodic tiling that ships, and MultigridNoise ships beside it as the cheap arrangement node. Everything else in the family is a mode, a graph or a showcase.

QuasiTile. The candidate bound is real. I re-ran an independent forward de Bruijn construction in double precision (every rhomb enumerated from line crossings, random rotation, gamma in [-2,2), no candidate restriction): N=4..9, exactly one rhomb per point, zero hits outside {floor t, ceil t} over 1M points per N in the earlier run and 18k per N in my re-run, max |a - t| at N=5 0.620 against the analytic 0.647. The float32 bounded Locate disagreed on 0 to 16 of 1M points, all rounding at tile edges. So 4 candidates per pair, 40 at N=5, is correct, and the prototyper's numbers reproduce. Seeds 7 and 11 at wide windows give the same Penrose floor. Disagreement: the prototyper's 5.54x perlin scalar ratio is for the branchy hit test; with the recommended margin selection the harness gives 433 ns = 8.2x perlin2 and 3.75x worley2 5x5. The AVX2 figure is an estimate either way; I would say 15-45 ns in 2D N=5 (28:1 and 10:1 scalings), 3D heavy, and no 4D so GenTileable2D will not tile. Ship with that stated. The best new image is the tile-centre Lookup as relief: stepped Penrose terraces, more terrain-like than anything else here.

MultigridNoise. The long-line complaint is real and the idea's LineJitter does nothing: at N=7 seed 3 longest straight run is 86.8 units with no breaker and 86.8 with line offset J=.25 and J=.45 (88% of edge pixels on runs over 8 units), matching the earlier N=5 seed 42 run (90.4 vs 88-90). Polyline wander (8.2 units, 0.1%) and a plain Perlin domain warp (10.8 units, 0.9%) both fix it, so the breaker is a convenience; plain DomainWarp in a graph already solves it. Check: plain mosaic c0ratio 1.0 by design, leaded phason 7.91, far coords and 3D fine. Harness 3.0x perlin plain, 6x with phason (harness is map-lookup dominated; the prototyper's 2 ns direct kernel is plausible, AVX2 still an estimate). The relief is not terrain; my lookup-at-dual-vertex plateau attempt gave plates with a raised grout ridge network and was not adopted. One correction to the prototyper's framing: Parity N=4 and lattice distance N=4 can be built from existing nodes by the same 4D cut as below, but N=5 and N=7 cannot be reached by any graph, and the O(N) analytic form is far cheaper than a 4D source.

FFT. Spots are there and are fine: QuasiTile vertex distance has clear 10-fold Bragg spots, multigrid lattice distance N=5 and N=7 show sharp spot lattices, and the region-hash outputs show a star from the straight lines that disappears with wander or phason. Nothing in the FFTs argues against shipping.

DomainQuasicrystal is a graph recipe, which the prototyper did not say: AddDimension(AddDimension(Checkerboard, Gradient(.7071,.7071)), Gradient(-.7071,.7071)) rendered with fnlab on the real DLL gives the same octagonal star ornament as the prototype. Drop the idea, keep the graph as an example.

SubstitutionTiling: showcase, not promising-for-ship. Seed 3 shows the same two dominant streak directions as the prototyper's sheet, so the direction bias is structural at affordable depth; Robinson stop=0 is periodic with broken half rhombs; the mixed-depth shard looks are striking but the crack family BSP covers that ground. PhasonWaves is the WaveSum mode of MultigridNoise (ship-as-mode). QuasiFold is a striking effect (seed 3 same look, 7.3x perlin with ridged source) with blurry facets and weak 3D; showcase, to be weighed against domain-kaleidoscope.

So: two nodes, QuasiTile (2D/3D, N in {4,5,7}, Output {EdgeDistance, TileValue, TileType, Grouted, Bevel, TypePavers, CentreLookup}) and MultigridNoise (2D/3D/4D, Output {RegionValue, EdgeDistance, Grouted, Parity, LatticeDistance, WaveSum, Lookup}, breaker = polyline wander or phason, never the line offset). All AVX2 costs remain estimates; no port exists.
families.proto_answer:
Ship MultigridNoise first and QuasiTile second, as two nodes. Hold SubstitutionTiling as promising, do not ship Robinson as the Penrose route, and do not ship DomainQuasicrystal.

WHY TWO NODES. MultigridNoise is the cheap building block: about 1 ns (estimate), direct scalar Mosaic 2.0 ns measured against harness perlin2 at 50.2 ns. It works in 2D, 3D and 4D, including the torus map, and has an exact edge distance. It does not look like tiles: it has X-junctions and infinite lines. QuasiTile is the only thing here that gives true Penrose tiles, with no line problem, but it costs about 20x as much (15-25 ns, estimate) and has no 4D form. The looks and the costs are different enough to keep them separate.

BOUND, VERIFIED BY BRUTE FORCE. The idea's 90 candidates are too many: 4 per pair suffice, so 40 for N=5, 24 for N=4, 84 for N=7. With the zonogon centred, the analytic bound on |a - t_j| is below 1 at every N.
- Bound vs largest seen: N=4 .6036 / .5969, N=5 .6472 / .6173, N=7 .6420 / .5708, N=9 .6399 / .5558.
- The wide search (about +-2-3 lines around the estimate) and the bounded search disagreed 0 times, over 1e6 random points with 40 random gamma sets for N=4 and 5, and 2e5 points for N=7 and 9.
- The few 0-hit and double-hit samples are float32 rounding, not a bound failure (N=5: 8 and 8 in 1e6). In double precision, 1e6 samples each at N=4, 5 and 7 all gave exactly 1 hit.
- True Penrose confirmed: thick:thin area 2.6194 (phi^2 is 2.6180), and with zero-sum gamma the vertex index census gives only 1 and 2 (149896, 150104 of 300000).
- Singular gamma (all zero) gave 0.38% bad samples, so a guard is needed.
- 3D 6-grid: 160 candidates, bound .809, seen .6973, 59999 of 60000 one hit, 1 double hit, volume ratio 2.6258. Forgetting the zonotope centre gave 1.05 and would break the bound.
- Float32 limit, bad samples (0 hits, double hits and wrong single tile) by distance in tile edges: .0003% at 100, .06% at 1e3, .16% at 1e4, .45% at 3e4, 1.8% at 1e5, 13.9% at 1e6.
- Choosing the candidate with the largest margin always returns one tile. It hides the defects rather than fixing them: clean by eye at 3e4, a few specks in the hillshade at 1e5. Its SIMD cost is an open question (branchy scalar prototype 365 vs 261 ns).

JITTER vs LONG STRAIGHT LINES. The idea's LineJitter fails, measured and by eye. Metric: 64 unit window, longest straight run of edge pixels.
- No breaker: 90.2 units.
- Line offset J=.45: 90.4 units, and the share of edge pixels on runs over 8 units rose from 62.7% to 73.6%. Lines look more obvious because the regular interference is gone.
- At equal edge coverage (half width .0185) on two seeds, runs are 90.2/89.6 with no breaker and 89.3/89.3 with offset jitter. Share on long runs: 43.1/21.0% vs 36.5/35.5%.

What does work, at that same coverage on two seeds, all with 0.0% of edge pixels on runs over 8 units:
- Per-line polyline wander J=.45 L=2: 6.8/7.0 units.
- Phason J=.9 L=5: 7.4/7.2 units.
- Plain domain warp control J=.9 L=5: 7.6/8.0 units.

So plain DomainWarp in a graph already solves the complaint. Polyline wander is worth adding because it keeps straight-edged polygons. True tilings do not have the problem: QuasiTile 2.4 units at N=5, 2.3 at N=4, Robinson 2.7. Other seeds were only run for the multigrid rows.

FFT. Spots are present and fine: QuasiTile vertex distance shows clear 10-fold spots, and Multigrid lattice distance N=5 and N=7 show sharp spots. Region-hash outputs show a star instead, which is the lines themselves; the star arms disappear with wander or phason.

WHY NOT THE OTHERS.
- Robinson gives the same floor cheaper (direct scalar 151.6 vs 222.0 ns), but stop=0 is exactly periodic: top lattice translation kept tile type and edge distance at 100.00% of samples at D=8 and D=12. Seed gives 100.00% identical geometry, so it is only an offset. Broken half rhombs cover 5.52% of area at D=6 and .26% at D=12.
- Pinwheel's headline claim failed at affordable depth. Angle shares over 24 bins peak at .139 at D=8 and .122 at D=10 (uniform .042), only 12 bins are ever used, and straight runs are 25-31 units. Its mixed-depth shards are the real value and look striking, so it stays promising and should be judged against the crack family.
- DomainQuasicrystal only shows order on Checkerboard, sine sums and Cellular J=0, and MultigridNoise produces the same looks directly without a 4D source. Its Decagonal and Dodecagonal tables use 4 of 5 and 4 of 6 families and visibly shear.

All AVX2 figures are estimates from op counts or scaled scalar timings; no port exists yet.
challenged: QuasiTile scalar_vs_perlin 5.54: that is the branchy hit test; with the recommended params (best=1 margin selection) the harness measures 433 ns = 8.22x perlin2 and 3.75x worley2

QuasiTile est_avx2 15-25 ns for 2D N=5 is optimistic as a single range: scaling worley2 scalar to CellularDistance AVX2 gives about 15 ns but the prototyper's own 10:1 rule gives about 43 ns; it is 15-45 ns, estimate only

DomainQuasicrystal 'MultigridNoise produces the same looks directly' understates the case: the octagonal Checkerboard ornament is already a two-node graph of existing nodes (AddDimension x2 with Gradient positions), verified by rendering it with fnlab on base.dll
MultigridNoise Parity and LatticeDistance at N=4 are reachable from existing nodes by the same 4D cut (at 4D source cost); only N=5 and N=7 are truly new
SubstitutionTiling 'promising': seed 3 wide window shows the same structural direction bias and long streaks, Robinson stop=0 is periodic; this is showcase material, not a candidate node
kernels: Direction table plus seed-derived gamma: used by MultigridNoise, QuasiTile, QuasiFold and the WaveSum mode. 2D N-fold, 3D 6 icosahedral axes, 4D star (cos a, sin a, cos m a, sin m a).
Family solve: t = dot(p, d_i) + gamma_i, k = Floor(t), f = t - k, the O(N) core of every MultigridNoise output, with optional per-line wander and shared phason offset.

Bounded dual tile locate: per-pair 2x2 inverse tables plus margin selection over 4 candidates per pair, 2D; 3x3 inverse tables over 8 candidates per triple, 3D. Includes the zonogon centre in the estimate.
Phason offset: 2/3/4 noise evals applied per family through a perpendicular star table, reusable by WaveSum and all region outputs.
Substitution descent with frozen mask for hashed stop depth, shared by Pinwheel, Robinson and Prism3.

families.answer:
Does K-limited selection pop? No. I confirmed this in 2D and 3D, and in a 4D form I wrote myself, which the prototyper never did. The test scans a field, then bisects the worst neighbour pairs until only a true jump would keep its size, with the fade switched off as a positive control.
- 2D: 80 configs (R up to 1.5, analytic mean overlap 7.07). Worst leftover step .0049 against 1.985 with the fade off.
- 3D: 36 configs (mean overlap up to 14.1, max 19). .0023 against 1.87.
- 4D: 12 configs, stripes source only (mean overlap up to 25, max 33). .0019 against 1.87.
- The steepest case shrinks 8x with 8x finer h, so it is a slope, not a jump. In the moving-slice pop map only the fade-off panels show bright arcs: largest frame change .902 off, .173.
- Weighted mean does jump (2.00 at K=1), so the prototyper is right to exclude it.

Where I disagree on stamp-scatter:
- The thinning is mostly caused by the rank-subtract formula, not by K limiting. By continuity, all weights must vanish only at an exact K+1 way tie, because any of those stamps could be the one dropped. That is an algebraic argument, not a measurement.
- Rank subtract also weakens stamps that are not tied. My cascade fade thins a stamp only when it is tied with the rank below. It needs the same source evals, plus one min and one multiply per slot.
